# IMAC downgrades

These descriptions are generated from the Tuning package of FCScore and describe what FCScore measures for each downgrade. See the [downgrade reference](index.md) for how to read them.

Generated from Tuning commit: `b86030c`.

**Rulebook source**

> - [AMA RC Scale Aerobatics Competition Regulations 2026-2027](https://www.modelaircraft.org/sites/default/files/events/rule-books/2026/RC_Scale_Aerobatics_2026-2027.pdf)
>
> Section II of this document is the Scale Aerobatics Official Flying and Judging Guide, which IMAC uses. The references in `judging_guide.json` are verbatim extracts from Section II, and `paragraph` is the Section II paragraph number (for example `Section II, 8.5` is the Stall Turns criteria and `Section II, 4.3` is the Airspace Control Score). The paragraph number is followed by the sub-item letter where the criteria are lettered.
>
> The older guide at https://mini-iac.hu/pdf/AMAScaleAerobaticsRulebook.pdf was not used. The IMAC site (www.mini-iac.org), which hosts the current Flying and Judging Guide and Contest Director's Guide, was not reachable when the references were written, so they should be checked against the latest edition published there.
>
> The guide does not define the dimensions of the aerobatic box and gives no per-figure downgrade for leaving it, so the FCScore box downgrades are estimates linked to the Airspace Control Score and the Deadline rules.

Rulebook extracts are quoted verbatim and listed under [Rulebook references](#rulebook-references).

## Intra-element downgrades

### Line Heading Drift {#track_z}

`track_z`

Checks that the flight path of each line stays on the template heading, with no sideways drift or turning away. Only growth in the heading error is charged, so a correction back towards the line is free. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, high or wide in the box, or on awkward line angles.

??? note "Details"

    Lines are judged on flight path, so the path over the ground must stay straight on the correct heading and be wind corrected. Any drift observed on any line, horizontal, 45° or vertical, is downgraded at 0.5 point for each 5°, but the attitude changes needed to hold the path are ignored.

    FCScore compares the direction of the aircraft's velocity with the template line and measures the sideways (heading) angle between them on each line. Each increase in the absolute error is charged and each decrease is free, so a drift that builds up costs points while correcting back does not, and an error already present when the line starts is not charged again because it was charged where it arose. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 10° of error, in line with the IMAC rule of 0.5 point for each 5°. The line between two figures belongs to the next figure, so what is measured on the exit line of a figure is reported with the following figure, and the figure's own score keeps the rest.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side, and when the correct line is at an angle that is hard to picture: horizontal and vertical lines are the easiest to judge, 45° lines are harder and the angles in between are hardest. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> All lines are judged in relation to the true horizon and the axes of the Aerobatic Airspace. Horizontal and Vertical lines are judged primarily on flight path (Ref Rule 5.3 for wind correction criteria).
>
> [Section II, 7.1](#rb-lines.flight_path)

> Wind correction shall be used throughout the aerobatic airspace. Any drift observed on any line (horizontal, 45 degrees or vertical) shall be downgraded using the 0.5 point deduction per 5 degrees rule
>
> [Section II, 5.3](#rb-general.drift)

### Line Pitch Drift {#track_y}

`track_y`

Checks that the flight path of each line stays at the template pitch, with no climbing, sinking or leaning away from the intended line. Only growth in the pitch error is charged, so a correction back towards the line is free. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, high or wide in the box, or on awkward line angles.

??? note "Details"

    Lines are judged on flight path, so the path must stay at the correct angle to the horizon, level on a horizontal line and truly vertical on an up- or down-line, and be wind corrected. Any drift observed on any line, horizontal, 45° or vertical, is downgraded at 0.5 point for each 5°.

    FCScore compares the direction of the aircraft's velocity with the template line and measures the angle between them in the pitch direction of the line (climbing or sinking on a horizontal line, leaning forwards or backwards on a vertical one). Each increase in the absolute error is charged and each decrease is free, and an error already present when the line starts is not charged again because it was charged where it arose. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 10° of error, in line with the IMAC rule of 0.5 point for each 5°. The line between two figures belongs to the next figure, so what is measured on the exit line of a figure is reported with the following figure, and the figure's own score keeps the rest.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side, and when the correct line is at an angle that is hard to picture: horizontal and vertical lines are the easiest to judge, 45° lines are harder and the angles in between are hardest. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> All lines are judged in relation to the true horizon and the axes of the Aerobatic Airspace. Horizontal and Vertical lines are judged primarily on flight path (Ref Rule 5.3 for wind correction criteria).
>
> [Section II, 7.1](#rb-lines.flight_path)

> Wind correction shall be used throughout the aerobatic airspace. Any drift observed on any line (horizontal, 45 degrees or vertical) shall be downgraded using the 0.5 point deduction per 5 degrees rule
>
> [Section II, 5.3](#rb-general.drift)

### Loop Plane Drift {#axial_track}

`axial_track`

Checks that the flight path of each loop or turn stays in its plane. For a vertical loop this is sideways drift out of the plane, for a turn it is climbing or sinking. Only growth in the angle is charged. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, or high or wide in the box.

??? note "Details"

    The finish point of a loop must not be displaced perpendicular to the plane of the loop, at 0.5 point per 5°, though visible crabbing in a heavy crosswind is not charged. In turns the altitude must stay constant, with variation charged at 0.5 point per 5°.

    FCScore measures the angle between the flight path and the plane of the loop, that is, the component of the flight path along the loop axis. Each increase in the absolute angle is charged and each decrease is free, so a drift that builds up costs points but correcting back does not. For a horizontal turn the loop axis is vertical, so the measure is the climb or descent of the flight path. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 10° of error, in line with the IMAC rule of 0.5 point for each 5°.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, and when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> Therefore, a standard deduction of 0.5 points per five (5) degrees shall be applied if the finish point is displaced in a direction perpendicular to the plane of the loop (Fig. 34). In a heavy crosswind situation, a loop might be flown with visible crabbing and no deduction shall be applied in this case.
>
> [Section II, 8.7.4a](#rb-loops.perpendicular)

> The aircraft must maintain a constant altitude throughout the figure. Any variation would be 0.5 point deduction for every 5 degrees of change.
>
> [Section II, 8.2.1 d](#rb-turns.altitude)

### Loop Exit Flight Path {#radial_track}

`radial_track`

Checks that the flight path at the end of each loop points in the intended direction within the plane of the loop. The full angle error at the end of the loop is charged once. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, high or wide in the box, or on awkward line angles.

??? note "Details"

    A loop or part-loop must finish on the line the figure requires, judged on flight path. If the aircraft does not return to the correct flight path, any deviation to the line of the next element is charged to the figure in progress.

    FCScore takes the last point of the loop and charges the whole angle between the flight path and the template within the plane of the loop. It is an absolute measure at the end of the loop, so an over- or under-flown arc is charged here once and the line that follows is only charged for further change. It applies to loops that are not part of a continuous sequence of loops. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 10° of error, in line with the IMAC rule of 0.5 point for each 5°.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side, and when the correct line is at an angle that is hard to picture: horizontal and vertical lines are the easiest to judge, 45° lines are harder and the angles in between are hardest. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> All lines are judged in relation to the true horizon and the axes of the Aerobatic Airspace. Horizontal and Vertical lines are judged primarily on flight path (Ref Rule 5.3 for wind correction criteria).
>
> [Section II, 7.1](#rb-lines.flight_path)

> If an aircraft does not return to wings-level, horizontal flight at the end of one fuselage length when exiting a figure, any deviation from wings level horizontal flight to the track on the line of the following figure MUST be deducted from the score of the figure in progress using the ½ point per 5 degrees rule.
>
> [Section II, 6.2](#rb-lines.figure_exit)

### Roll Angle on Lines {#line_roll_angle}

`line_roll_angle`

Checks that the wings stay at the correct attitude on lines without a roll, and during stall turns and tailslides. Only growth in the roll angle error is charged, so levelling the wings again is free. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: when you are looking at the top or underside of the aircraft, when it is high or wide in the box, or at awkward bank angles.

??? note "Details"

    Any bank angle of the wing in the roll axis is downgraded at 0.5 point for each 5°, and in a stall turn there must be no roll deviation during the pivot. In a tailslide the roll attitude must stay perpendicular to the plane of the main axis of flight, including during the fall-through.

    FCScore measures the roll angle relative to the template on lines that contain no roll, and through stall turns and tailslides, and charges each increase in the absolute roll error; a decrease is free. An angle already present at the start of the element is not charged again because it was charged where it arose. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 10° of error, in line with the IMAC rule of 0.5 point for each 5°. The line between two figures belongs to the next figure, so what is measured on the exit line of a figure is reported with the following figure, and the figure's own score keeps the rest.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. Roll errors are easiest to see when the aircraft is viewed side-on and hardest when you are looking at its top or underside. They are also harder to judge when the aircraft is high in the box or far to one side, and when the bank angle or the line is awkward to picture: wings level, knife-edge and inverted are the easiest references, with the angles in between the hardest. A fixed balancing factor, smaller than for flight path errors, further reduces small roll errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> On the other hand, any bank angle of the wing in the roll axis should be downgraded using the standard rule of 0.5 point deduction per 5 degrees
>
> [Section II, 5.3](#rb-general.bank)

> During the pivot, the wings must remain in the vertical geometric plane as dictated by the ARESTI. This alignment must be maintained throughout the pivot, and the aircraft’s attitude at the beginning and the ending of the pivot must be absolutely vertical. During the pivot there must be no deviation in pitch or roll. Any pitch and roll deviation observed during the pivot shall be downgraded at 0.5 points for each 5 degrees of deviation.
>
> [Section II, 8.5](#rb-stall_turns.pivot_attitude)

> On all up and down lines, the roll attitude must be perpendicular to the plane of the main axis of flight, either the X or Y axis. This includes the duration of the fall through. Watch for the aircraft torqueing off the correct plane of flight. Any deviation in roll shall be downgraded at 0.5 points per five (5) degrees of deviation.
>
> [Section II, 8.6 c](#rb-tailslides.roll)

### Roll Angle in Loops {#loop_roll_angle}

`loop_roll_angle`

Checks that the wings stay in the plane of the loop when there is no roll. Only growth in the roll angle error is charged, so levelling the wings again is free. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: when you are looking at the top or underside of the aircraft, when it is high or wide in the box, or at awkward bank angles.

??? note "Details"

    A loop that has no roll element must be flown without any roll; any roll other than during a roll element on the loop is downgraded at 0.5 point per 5°.

    FCScore measures the roll angle relative to the template in vertical loops that contain no roll, and charges each increase in the absolute roll error; a decrease is free. An angle already present at the start of the loop is not charged again. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 10° of error, in line with the IMAC rule of 0.5 point for each 5°.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. Roll errors are easiest to see when the aircraft is viewed side-on and hardest when you are looking at its top or underside. They are also harder to judge when the aircraft is high in the box or far to one side, and when the bank angle or the line is awkward to picture: wings level, knife-edge and inverted are the easiest references, with the angles in between the hardest. A fixed balancing factor, smaller than for flight path errors, further reduces small roll errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> Aircraft displaying any roll other than during a roll element on the loop, 0.5 point per five degrees of roll.
>
> [Section II, 8.7.4a](#rb-loops.roll)

### Roll Angle in Rolling Turn Pauses {#circle_pause_roll_angle}

`circle_pause_roll_angle`

Checks that the wings stay at the template attitude during a brief pause between the rolls of a rolling turn. Only growth in the roll angle error is charged, so returning to the attitude is free. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: when you are looking at the top or underside of the aircraft, when it is high or wide in the box, or at awkward bank angles.

??? note "Details"

    A rolling turn may include a brief pause between its rolls. Any bank angle of the wing in the roll axis that is not part of a roll element is downgraded at 0.5 point per 5°.

    FCScore measures the roll angle relative to the template on the short level loop segments that sit between two rolling segments of a turn, and charges each increase in the absolute roll error; a decrease is free. An angle already present at the start of the pause is not charged again. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 10° of error, in line with the IMAC rule of 0.5 point for each 5°.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. Roll errors are easiest to see when the aircraft is viewed side-on and hardest when you are looking at its top or underside. They are also harder to judge when the aircraft is high in the box or far to one side, and when the bank angle or the line is awkward to picture: wings level, knife-edge and inverted are the easiest references, with the angles in between the hardest. A fixed balancing factor, smaller than for flight path errors, further reduces small roll errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> On the other hand, any bank angle of the wing in the roll axis should be downgraded using the standard rule of 0.5 point deduction per 5 degrees
>
> [Section II, 5.3](#rb-general.bank)

### Bank Angle in Turns {#turn_roll_angle}

`turn_roll_angle`

Checks that the bank angle established for a turn is held. Only growth in the bank angle error during the turn is charged, so returning to the bank is free. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: when you are looking at the top or underside of the aircraft, when it is high or wide in the box, or at awkward bank angles.

??? note "Details"

    Once the bank angle of a turn is established it must remain constant, with any deviation downgraded at 0.5 point for every 5°. It must be between 60° and 90°.

    FCScore measures how the bank angle differs from the angle established at the start of the turn, taking an established bank below 60° or above 90° as 60° or 90°, and charges each increase in the absolute error; a decrease is free. It applies to turns that contain no roll. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 10° of error, in line with the IMAC rule of 0.5 point for each 5°.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. Roll errors are easiest to see when the aircraft is viewed side-on and hardest when you are looking at its top or underside. They are also harder to judge when the aircraft is high in the box or far to one side, and when the bank angle or the line is awkward to picture: wings level, knife-edge and inverted are the easiest references, with the angles in between the hardest. A fixed balancing factor, smaller than for flight path errors, further reduces small roll errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> The angle of bank, once established, must remain constant. Any deviation is a 0.5 point deduction for every 5 degrees of deviation.
>
> [Section II, 8.2.1 b](#rb-turns.bank)

### Roll Rotation Amount {#roll_roll_angle}

`roll_roll_angle`

Checks that a roll, snap or spin finishes at the planned attitude. At the point of maximum rotation, the roll attitude is compared with the planned attitude and the difference is charged once, so both over- and under-rotation count. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: when you are looking at the top or underside of the aircraft, when it is high or wide in the box, or at awkward bank angles.

??? note "Details"

    A roll must stop precisely after the desired degree of rotation, and under- or over-rotating costs 0.5 point per 5°, including 'bumping the point' by going past the stop and returning. A spin must complete precisely at the rotation called for, short or long.

    FCScore finds the point of maximum rotation in each roll, snap or spin and compares the aircraft's roll attitude there with the planned attitude. It assesses the final attitude, not the total number of degrees rolled, although it tracks the rotation continuously (allowing for the angle wrapping round at 180°) so that a roll that overshoots by a full turn is not mistaken for a correct one. Over-rotation and under-rotation are charged equally, as a single absolute error at that point. Rolling back afterwards is charged separately. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 10° of error, in line with the IMAC rule of 0.5 point for each 5°.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. Roll errors are easiest to see when the aircraft is viewed side-on and hardest when you are looking at its top or underside. They are also harder to judge when the aircraft is high in the box or far to one side, and when the bank angle or the line is awkward to picture: wings level, knife-edge and inverted are the easiest references, with the angles in between the hardest. A fixed balancing factor, smaller than for flight path errors, further reduces small roll errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> The wing must stop precisely after the desired degree of rotation and not go past the stop point and then return. This is referred to as “bumping the point” and a deduction of 0.5 points per 5 degrees shall be given in this case.
>
> [Section II, 8.9.1](#rb-rolls.stop)

> Errors in degrees of rotation (under/over rotating the points) are downgraded at a half (.5) point per five (5) degrees.
>
> [Section II, 8.9.2](#rb-rolls.point_rotation)

> The spin element must complete precisely at the degree of rotation called for by the ARESTI and not be short or beyond the prescribed end point of the rotation. Any deviation is to be downgraded 0.5 points per 5 degrees that the aircraft completes the spin short or long of the prescribed stopping point.
>
> [Section II, 8.9.4 g](#rb-spins.stop)

### Turn Entry Bank Angle {#preturn_roll_angle}

`preturn_roll_angle`

Checks that the roll into a turn establishes at least 60° of bank. Any shortfall below 60° at the end of the roll is charged once. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: when you are looking at the top or underside of the aircraft, when it is high or wide in the box, or at awkward bank angles.

??? note "Details"

    The angle of bank established by the initial roll of a turn must be at least 60° and not more than 90°; any less or more costs 0.5 point for every 5°.

    FCScore takes the point of maximum rotation of the roll that precedes a turn, measures the bank angle from wings level, and charges any amount by which it is below 60°. A bank above 90° is not possible to measure this way, so only a shortfall is charged. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 10° of error, in line with the IMAC rule of 0.5 point for each 5°.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. Roll errors are easiest to see when the aircraft is viewed side-on and hardest when you are looking at its top or underside. They are also harder to judge when the aircraft is high in the box or far to one side, and when the bank angle or the line is awkward to picture: wings level, knife-edge and inverted are the easiest references, with the angles in between the hardest. A fixed balancing factor, smaller than for flight path errors, further reduces small roll errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> The angle of bank established by the initial rolling maneuver must be at least 60 degrees and not greater than 90 degrees. Any less or more is a 0.5 point deduction for every 5 degrees.
>
> [Section II, 8.2.1 a](#rb-turns.entry_bank)

### Roll Rebound {#rebound}

`rebound`

Checks that a roll stays where it stopped. After the maximum rotation, any growth in the roll error, such as bouncing back past the target or wobbling, is charged. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: when you are looking at the top or underside of the aircraft, when it is high or wide in the box, or at awkward bank angles.

??? note "Details"

    The wing must stop precisely after the desired rotation and not go past the stop point and then return; this is called 'bumping the point' and costs 0.5 point per 5°. The finish should be as crisp and precise as possible.

    FCScore looks at each rotating element after the point of maximum rotation and charges each increase in the absolute roll error. An over-rotation is charged once, at its maximum, and the return is free, but rolling back past the target or rocking the wings creates a new increase that is charged. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 10° of error, in line with the IMAC rule of 0.5 point for each 5°.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. Roll errors are easiest to see when the aircraft is viewed side-on and hardest when you are looking at its top or underside. They are also harder to judge when the aircraft is high in the box or far to one side, and when the bank angle or the line is awkward to picture: wings level, knife-edge and inverted are the easiest references, with the angles in between the hardest. A fixed balancing factor, smaller than for flight path errors, further reduces small roll errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> The wing must stop precisely after the desired degree of rotation and not go past the stop point and then return. This is referred to as “bumping the point” and a deduction of 0.5 points per 5 degrees shall be given in this case.
>
> [Section II, 8.9.1](#rb-rolls.stop)

> The finish of the roll must be as crisp and precise as possible. Coming to a slow finish in fact represents a change in the rate of roll and shall be penalized accordingly.
>
> [Section II, 8.9.1](#rb-rolls.finish)

### Roll Centring on the Loop {#loop_roll_centre}

`loop_roll_centre`

Checks that a roll, or roll combination, on a loop is centred on the apex or nadir. The angle between the middle of the rolling section and the apex is charged once for the whole section. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: loops viewed edge-on, and loops high or wide in the box.

??? note "Details"

    A rolling element (roll, point rolls or snap roll) at the apex of a loop must be centred in the loop and flown on the arc of the loop itself. If the roll is not centred it is downgraded 0.5 points for every five degrees that it is off centre, and flying the roll on a line at the apex is at least a two point downgrade.

    FCScore takes the whole rolling section of one loop as a single window: the rolls and snaps and the pauses between them, but not the loop flown either side of it. It reads the flight path elevation where the section starts and where it ends. The path falls through the top of a loop and rises through the bottom, so the average of the two elevations is zero when the section is centred about the apex or nadir, whatever the size and shape of the loop (round, P, Q or reversing) and however much of it the pilot uses. An error of 10° in where the roll sits on the loop is a 10° error in that average. FCScore charges its size once, at the end of the section, as an angle, so a roll centred early and one centred late cost the same. It is measured from the flown path, so a roll that misses the apex altogether is still charged for how far from it it was. Rolls and snaps on straight lines are not covered, and neither are loops whose roll fills the whole loop element, which have no apex to centre on. The extra deduction for flying part of a roll on a straight line is not measured here. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 10° of error, in line with the IMAC rule of 0.5 point for each 5°.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. Where a roll sits on a loop is easiest to judge when the loop is viewed face-on (the judge looking along the loop's axis) and hardest when it is seen edge-on, where the position along the loop is hidden. It is also harder to judge high in the box or far to one side. The weighting does not depend on how much of the loop the roll uses. Large errors are counted in full.

> If there is a rolling element (roll, point rolls or snap roll) at the apex of the loop, it must be centered in the loop and flown on the arc of the loop itself (Fig. 38). Flying the roll on a line at the apex of the loop is at least a two (2) point downgrade. If the roll is not centered, it must be downgraded 0.5 points for every five degrees that it is off center.
>
> [Section II, 8.7.4a](#rb-loops.integrated_rolls)

### Snap Centring on the Loop {#loop_snap_centre}

`loop_snap_centre`

Checks that a snap roll on a loop is centred on the apex or nadir. The angle between the middle of the rolling section and the apex is charged once for the whole section. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: loops viewed edge-on, and loops high or wide in the box.

??? note "Details"

    A snap roll on a loop is part of the same rolling section as the rolls on that loop, and the whole section must be centred about the apex or nadir. The snap is not scored separately: FCScore scores the rolls, snaps and pauses of the loop together as one window, under the roll centring downgrade (loop_roll_centre), and this key is only used to join the snap into it. A loop whose only roll is a snap is scored in the same way, with the snap centred on the apex.

    FCScore takes the whole rolling section of one loop as a single window: the rolls and snaps and the pauses between them, but not the loop flown either side of it. It reads the flight path elevation where the section starts and where it ends. The path falls through the top of a loop and rises through the bottom, so the average of the two elevations is zero when the section is centred about the apex or nadir, whatever the size and shape of the loop (round, P, Q or reversing) and however much of it the pilot uses. An error of 10° in where the roll sits on the loop is a 10° error in that average. FCScore charges its size once, at the end of the section, as an angle, so a roll centred early and one centred late cost the same. It is measured from the flown path, so a roll that misses the apex altogether is still charged for how far from it it was. Rolls and snaps on straight lines are not covered, and neither are loops whose roll fills the whole loop element, which have no apex to centre on. The extra deduction for flying part of a roll on a straight line is not measured here. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 10° of error, in line with the IMAC rule of 0.5 point for each 5°.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. Where a roll sits on a loop is easiest to judge when the loop is viewed face-on (the judge looking along the loop's axis) and hardest when it is seen edge-on, where the position along the loop is hidden. It is also harder to judge high in the box or far to one side. The weighting does not depend on how much of the loop the roll uses. Large errors are counted in full.

> If there is a rolling element (roll, point rolls or snap roll) at the apex of the loop, it must be centered in the loop and flown on the arc of the loop itself (Fig. 38). Flying the roll on a line at the apex of the loop is at least a two (2) point downgrade. If the roll is not centered, it must be downgraded 0.5 points for every five degrees that it is off center.
>
> [Section II, 8.7.4a](#rb-loops.integrated_rolls)

### Pause Centring on the Loop {#loop_pause_centre}

`loop_pause_centre`

Checks that a pause between rolls on a loop is centred on the apex or nadir. The angle between the middle of the rolling section and the apex is charged once for the whole section. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: loops viewed edge-on, and loops high or wide in the box.

??? note "Details"

    A pause between two rolls or snaps on a loop is part of the same rolling section as the rolls on that loop, and the whole section must be centred about the apex or nadir. The pause is not scored separately: FCScore scores the rolls, snaps and pauses of the loop together as one window, under the roll centring downgrade (loop_roll_centre), and this key is only used to join the pause into it. The pads of the loop before and after the rolling section are not part of it.

    FCScore takes the whole rolling section of one loop as a single window: the rolls and snaps and the pauses between them, but not the loop flown either side of it. It reads the flight path elevation where the section starts and where it ends. The path falls through the top of a loop and rises through the bottom, so the average of the two elevations is zero when the section is centred about the apex or nadir, whatever the size and shape of the loop (round, P, Q or reversing) and however much of it the pilot uses. An error of 10° in where the roll sits on the loop is a 10° error in that average. FCScore charges its size once, at the end of the section, as an angle, so a roll centred early and one centred late cost the same. It is measured from the flown path, so a roll that misses the apex altogether is still charged for how far from it it was. Rolls and snaps on straight lines are not covered, and neither are loops whose roll fills the whole loop element, which have no apex to centre on. The extra deduction for flying part of a roll on a straight line is not measured here. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 10° of error, in line with the IMAC rule of 0.5 point for each 5°.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. Where a roll sits on a loop is easiest to judge when the loop is viewed face-on (the judge looking along the loop's axis) and hardest when it is seen edge-on, where the position along the loop is hidden. It is also harder to judge high in the box or far to one side. The weighting does not depend on how much of the loop the roll uses. Large errors are counted in full.

> If there is a rolling element (roll, point rolls or snap roll) at the apex of the loop, it must be centered in the loop and flown on the arc of the loop itself (Fig. 38). Flying the roll on a line at the apex of the loop is at least a two (2) point downgrade. If the roll is not centered, it must be downgraded 0.5 points for every five degrees that it is off center.
>
> [Section II, 8.7.4a](#rb-loops.integrated_rolls)

### Roll Rate Consistency {#roll_rate}

`roll_rate`

Checks that the roll rate is constant through each roll. The size of the variation in roll rate, compared with the average, is charged once for the roll. Small variations are discounted when they are hard to see: when you are looking at the top or underside of the aircraft, when it is high or wide in the box, and for short part-rolls that give less to judge.

??? note "Details"

    The rate of roll must be constant throughout the roll, and each variation costs one point. Coming to a slow finish is itself a change in the rate of roll and is penalised.

    FCScore measures the roll rate throughout each roll and calculates how much it varies as a fraction of its average. A steady roll scores zero, whatever its rate. The more the rate varies, the larger the downgrade, in proportion rather than in whole points per variation.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. Roll rate is easier to see when the aircraft is viewed side-on than when you are looking at its top or underside, and easier in front of the judge than high in the box or far to one side. The weighting also grows with the amount of roll flown: a full roll or more counts fully, a half roll counts about half, because short rolls give the judge less to assess. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors.

> In all cases, the same criteria apply: the rate of roll must be constant throughout the roll(s). The aircraft shall continue to project, during the rolling portion, the prescribed plane and direction of flight.
>
> [Section II, 8.9](#rb-rolls.constant_rate)

> The penalty for varying the rate of roll is one (1) point per variation. Any stoppage in the roll that could result its being considered a point roll would zero (0) the figure.
>
> [Section II, 8.9.1](#rb-rolls.rate)

### Roll Pauses {#roll_excitation}

`roll_excitation`

Checks that the roll does not stop partway. The share of the roll for which the roll rate is close to zero, or reversed, is charged. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see (aircraft viewed from above or below, or high or wide in the box) and short rotations count for less.

??? note "Details"

    A roll must not stop: a stoppage that could make it look like a point roll zeroes the figure, and in a rolling turn each stoppage of the rate of roll costs one point.

    FCScore counts the time during each roll in which the roll rate is effectively zero or reversed. A rate below about 1.5° per second counts as fully stopped, a rate above about 3° per second counts as moving, and values in between count partly. The downgrade is based on the fraction of the roll's duration spent stopped, so a long hold costs more than a brief one.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. A stop in the rotation is easier to see when the aircraft is viewed side-on than from above or below, and easier in front of the judge than high in the box or far to one side. The weighting is also scaled by the amount of rotation flown, so a short rotation counts for less than a full one.

> The penalty for varying the rate of roll is one (1) point per variation. Any stoppage in the roll that could result its being considered a point roll would zero (0) the figure.
>
> [Section II, 8.9.1](#rb-rolls.rate)

> Each stoppage of the rate of roll is a deduction of one (1) point.
>
> [Section II, 8.2.2 c](#rb-turns.rolling_stoppage)

### Loop Roundness {#radius}

`radius`

Checks that each loop is round, with a constant radius throughout. The variation of the radius within the loop, compared with its average, is charged once for the loop. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: loops viewed edge-on, high or wide in the box, and part-loops that show less of the shape.

??? note "Details"

    All radii must be constant, and each visible variation in the radius of a loop or part-loop costs one point. The size of the loop is not a grading criterion.

    FCScore fits a circle to the flown path of the loop in the plane of the loop and measures how much the aircraft's distance from the fitted centre varies, as a fraction of the average radius. A perfectly round loop scores zero, whatever its size, and the more the radius varies the larger the downgrade, charged in proportion rather than in whole points per variation.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. Shape errors are easiest to see when the loop is viewed face-on (the judge looking along the loop's axis) and hardest when it is seen edge-on, where distortions are hidden. They are also harder to judge high in the box or far to one side, and the weighting is scaled by how much of a full loop is flown: a complete loop counts fully, a quarter loop about a quarter. Large errors are counted in full.

> All radii are to be constant. Each visible variation in the radii in a loop or part loop is to be downgraded by one (1) point. Flight path without any radius (straight line or “flat spot”), is deducted at one point per occurrence.
>
> [Section II, 8.7.1 b](#rb-loops.constant_radius)

> The size of a loop or part loop is not a grading criterion.
>
> [Section II, 8.7.1 a](#rb-loops.size)

### Flat Spots in Loops {#radius_excitation}

`radius_excitation`

Checks that the loop has no straight sections. The share of the loop for which the flight path is effectively straight is charged. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: when the loop is high or wide in the box, when the direction towards the loop centre lies along the line of sight, and for part-loops that show less of the shape.

??? note "Details"

    Flight path without any radius, a straight line or 'flat spot', is deducted at one point per occurrence.

    FCScore watches the curvature of the flight path through the loop and counts the time during which it is effectively straight, or curving the wrong way. A local radius of about 1000 m or more counts as fully flat and about 500 m or less counts as curved, with values in between counting partly. The downgrade is based on the fraction of the loop's duration that is flat.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. These errors are easier to see when the direction from the aircraft towards the centre of the loop lies across the judge's line of sight, and harder when it lies along it. They are also harder to judge high in the box or far to one side, and the weighting is scaled by how much of a full loop is flown: a complete loop counts fully, a quarter loop about a quarter.

> All radii are to be constant. Each visible variation in the radii in a loop or part loop is to be downgraded by one (1) point. Flight path without any radius (straight line or “flat spot”), is deducted at one point per occurrence.
>
> [Section II, 8.7.1 b](#rb-loops.constant_radius)

### Loop Rate of Turn {#curvature}

`curvature`

Checks that the loop keeps a steady rate of turn for its speed. The variation in the loop's curvature, compared with its average, is charged once for the loop. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: when the loop is high or wide in the box, when the direction towards the loop centre lies along the line of sight, and for part-loops that show less of the shape.

??? note "Details"

    All radii must be constant. As the speed changes in a loop the rate of turn has to change with it to keep the radius constant, so the aircraft should neither tighten nor open up as it goes round.

    FCScore measures the rate of turn divided by the speed of travel (the curvature, which is one over the radius) throughout the loop and calculates how much it varies as a fraction of its average. Because it is based on how quickly the aircraft is turning for its speed, it picks up a tightening or opening of the loop early. The more the curvature varies, the larger the downgrade.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. These errors are easier to see when the direction from the aircraft towards the centre of the loop lies across the judge's line of sight, and harder when it lies along it. They are also harder to judge high in the box or far to one side, and the weighting is scaled by how much of a full loop is flown: a complete loop counts fully, a quarter loop about a quarter.

> All radii are to be constant. Each visible variation in the radii in a loop or part loop is to be downgraded by one (1) point. Flight path without any radius (straight line or “flat spot”), is deducted at one point per occurrence.
>
> [Section II, 8.7.1 b](#rb-loops.constant_radius)

### Spin Rotation Axis {#spin_rotation_axis}

`spin_rotation_axis`

Checks that the spin is a true autorotation rather than an aileron-type roll. Time spent rotating about an axis too close to the fuselage line, below 20°, is charged. Small errors are discounted only for aircraft that are high or wide in the box, where the angle is harder to judge.

??? note "Details"

    A spin must be an autorotation, which has a visible yaw component. Without it the aircraft is probably in some kind of aileron roll, and if the judge is certain that no autorotation occurred the figure is zeroed.

    FCScore measures the angle between the fuselage axis and the axis the aircraft is rotating about, from 15° after the break to 45° before the end of the rotation. Any period in which it is below 20° looks like a roll about the fuselage rather than an autorotation and is charged, according to how far below the limit it is and how large a share of the spin it covers. The 20° threshold is an FCScore way of detecting autorotation, not a number given in the rules.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. The visibility factors are the aircraft's position in the box (errors are harder to judge high in the box or far to one side) and a fixed balancing factor. Large errors are counted in full.

> The rotation in a spin must be autorotation which can be difficult to discern. A clue to making the judgment on "autorotation or not" is that autorotation will have a visible yaw component to the rotation. Absent this yaw component, it is probable that the aircraft is in some kind of an aileron roll. If a judge is certain that no autorotation occurred, a zero (0) is to be given.
>
> [Section II, 8.9.4 f](#rb-spins.autorotation)

### Spin Nose Drop {#drop_pitch_rate}

`drop_pitch_rate`

Checks that the nose drops as the aircraft stalls into the spin. Time spent dropping slower than 6° per second in the first 15° of rotation is charged. Small shortfalls are discounted when hard to see: with the aircraft high or wide in the box, or directly above the judge.

??? note "Details"

    When the aircraft stalls the nose falls and, at the same time, a wing tip drops in the direction of the spin. The two must occur simultaneously, or the entry is a 'late entry' and is downgraded.

    FCScore measures the nose-down pitch rate from the start of the spin until the first 15° of rotation is complete. Any period below 6° per second is charged, according to how far below it is and how large a share of that window it covers. The 6° per second figure is an FCScore threshold for a definite nose drop, not a number from the rules.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. The nose drop is harder to see when the aircraft is directly above the judge, and when it is high in the box or far to one side. A fixed balancing factor also scales the error. Large errors are counted in full.

> When the aircraft stalls, the nose will fall and at the same time a wing tip will drop in the direction of the spin initiating autorotation. The fall of the nose and the drop of the wing are to occur simultaneously. Failure to achieve this is to be considered a “late entry” and is to be downgraded.
>
> [Section II, 8.9.4](#rb-spins.stall_break)

### Spin Rotation Hesitation {#spin_excitation}

`spin_excitation`

Checks that the spin keeps rotating. The share of the spin for which the rotation rate is very low is charged. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see (aircraft viewed from above or below, or high or wide in the box) and short rotations count for less.

??? note "Details"

    Autorotation must carry to completion. Coming out of autorotation early and finishing the spin with ailerons costs 0.5 point per 5° of aileroning. The speed of autorotation is not a judging criterion.

    FCScore counts the time in each spin during which the rotation rate in the correct direction is close to zero or reversed. A rate below about 9° per second counts as fully stopped, a rate above about 17° per second counts as rotating, and values in between count partly. The downgrade is based on the fraction of the spin's duration spent stopped.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. A stop in the rotation is easier to see when the aircraft is viewed side-on than from above or below, and easier in front of the judge than high in the box or far to one side. The weighting is also scaled by the amount of rotation flown, so a short rotation counts for less than a full one.

> Note that autorotation must carry to completion. It is common to see a pilot come out of autorotation early and aileron to the finish of the spin. If this occurs a penalty of 0.5 points per 5 degrees is to be applied for the amount of “aileroning” used to complete the required rotation.
>
> [Section II, 8.9.4 g](#rb-spins.completion)

### Spin Exit Pitch Track {#spin_exit_track_y}

`spin_exit_track_y`

Checks that the flight path is vertical down at the end of the spin. The full pitch error between the flight path and the template downline is charged once. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, high or wide in the box, or on awkward line angles.

??? note "Details"

    After the prescribed turns the aircraft must stop rotating precisely on the prescribed heading and then a wind corrected vertical down line must be shown. Omitting the line costs a point.

    FCScore takes the last point of the spin and charges the whole angle between the direction the aircraft is travelling and the template downline in the pitch direction. It is an absolute measure at that point, based on the direction of travel (the flight path). FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 10° of error, in line with the IMAC rule of 0.5 point for each 5°.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side, and when the correct line is at an angle that is hard to picture: horizontal and vertical lines are the easiest to judge, 45° lines are harder and the angles in between are hardest. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> After completion of the prescribed number of turns, the aircraft must stop rotating precisely on the prescribed heading and then a wind corrected vertical down line must be shown.
>
> [Section II, 8.9.4](#rb-spins.stop_heading)

> Upon completion of the prescribed degree of rotation a vertical down line is to be shown. Omission of this line is to be downgraded one (1) point.
>
> [Section II, 8.9.4 h](#rb-spins.downline)

### Spin Exit Sideways Track {#spin_exit_track_z}

`spin_exit_track_z`

Checks that the flight path is not leaning sideways at the end of the spin. The full sideways error between the flight path and the template downline is charged once. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, or high or wide in the box.

??? note "Details"

    After the prescribed turns the aircraft must stop rotating precisely on the prescribed heading and then a wind corrected vertical down line must be shown.

    FCScore takes the last point of the spin and charges the whole angle between the direction the aircraft is travelling and the template downline in the sideways direction. It is an absolute measure at that point, based on the direction of travel (the flight path). FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 10° of error, in line with the IMAC rule of 0.5 point for each 5°.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, and when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> After completion of the prescribed number of turns, the aircraft must stop rotating precisely on the prescribed heading and then a wind corrected vertical down line must be shown.
>
> [Section II, 8.9.4](#rb-spins.stop_heading)

> Upon completion of the prescribed degree of rotation a vertical down line is to be shown. Omission of this line is to be downgraded one (1) point.
>
> [Section II, 8.9.4 h](#rb-spins.downline)

### Snap Rotation Axis {#snap_rotation_axis}

`snap_rotation_axis`

Checks that the snap is a true autorotation rather than an axial roll. Time spent rotating about an axis too close to the fuselage line, below 10°, is charged. Small errors are discounted only for aircraft that are high or wide in the box, where the angle is harder to judge.

??? note "Details"

    In autorotation the aircraft is rolling while also displaced from straight flight in both pitch and yaw. Lacking any observable yaw component the aircraft is rotating only on its roll axis and is not presenting a snap.

    FCScore measures the angle between the fuselage axis and the axis the aircraft is rotating about, from 15° after the start of the rotation to 90° before its end. Any period in which it is below 10° looks like an aileron roll and is charged, according to how far below the limit it is and how large a share of the snap it covers. The threshold is an FCScore way of detecting autorotation, not a number given in the rules.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. The visibility factors are the aircraft's position in the box (errors are harder to judge high in the box or far to one side) and a fixed balancing factor. Large errors are counted in full.

> Autorotation: State of flight in which the aircraft is rolling while also displaced from straight flight (or radius in loops and part loops) in both the pitch and yaw axes.
>
> [Section II, 8.9.3](#rb-snap_rolls.autorotation_definition)

> Autorotation may difficult to discern, but there will be a visible yaw displacement to the rotation. Lacking any observable yaw component, the aircraft will be rotating only on its roll axis and not presenting a snap.
>
> [Section II, 8.9.3 c](#rb-snap_rolls.yaw_component)

### Snap Rotation Hesitation {#snap_excitation}

`snap_excitation`

Checks that the snap keeps rotating. The share of the snap for which the rotation rate is low is charged. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see (aircraft viewed from above or below, or high or wide in the box) and short rotations count for less.

??? note "Details"

    Autorotation, once initiated, must be maintained to the prescribed finish point of the snap. Exiting autorotation early and completing the snap with ailerons costs 0.5 point for each 5° of rotation remaining.

    FCScore counts the time in each snap during which the rotation rate in the correct direction is low. A rate below about 30° per second counts as fully stopped, a rate above about 57° per second counts as rotating, and values in between count partly. The downgrade is based on the fraction of the snap's duration spent stopped.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. A stop in the rotation is easier to see when the aircraft is viewed side-on than from above or below, and easier in front of the judge than high in the box or far to one side. The weighting is also scaled by the amount of rotation flown, so a short rotation counts for less than a full one.

> Autorotation, once initiated, must be maintained to the prescribed finish point of the snap roll. Exiting autorotation early and completing the snap with ailerons is a common error. In these cases, a downgrade of 0.5 points for each 5 degrees of rotation remaining at the point the autorotation ends shall apply.
>
> [Section II, 8.9.3 f](#rb-snap_rolls.autorotation_maintained)

### Positive Snap Pitch Break {#pos_break_pr}

`pos_break_pr`

Checks that a positive snap starts with a clear pitch break. If the peak pitch rate in the first 15° of rotation never reaches 30° per second, the shortfall is charged. Small shortfalls are discounted when hard to see: when you are looking at the top or underside of the aircraft, or when it is high or wide in the box.

??? note "Details"

    There must be an observable departure in the pitch axis in the required direction of the snap, toward the canopy for a positive snap. If a judge is certain a proper snap was not executed, the figure is zeroed.

    FCScore looks at the pitch rate over the first 15° of the rotation and takes its largest absolute value. If that peak never reaches 30° per second the shortfall is charged. The 30° per second figure is an FCScore threshold for a clear break, not a number from the rules, and only the peak counts.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. Pitch rate is easier to see when the aircraft is viewed side-on than when you are looking at its top or underside, and easier in front of the judge than high in the box or far to one side. A fixed balancing factor also scales the error.

> There must be an observable departure in the pitch axis in the required direction of the snap.
>
> [Section II, 8.9.3 b](#rb-snap_rolls.pitch_departure)

### Negative Snap Pitch Break {#neg_break_pr}

`neg_break_pr`

Checks that a negative snap starts with a clear pitch break. The peak pitch rate in the first 15° of rotation is compared with a 30° per second threshold and any shortfall is charged. Small shortfalls are discounted when hard to see: when you are looking at the top or underside of the aircraft, or when it is high or wide in the box.

??? note "Details"

    There must be an observable departure in the pitch axis in the required direction of the snap, toward the wheels for a negative snap. All the other judging criteria are the same as for a positive snap.

    FCScore looks at the pitch rate over the first 15° of the rotation and compares its absolute value with a 30° per second threshold, charging any shortfall. The threshold is an FCScore value for a clear break, not a number from the rules.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. Pitch rate is easier to see when the aircraft is viewed side-on than when you are looking at its top or underside, and easier in front of the judge than high in the box or far to one side. A fixed balancing factor also scales the error.

> There must be an observable departure in the pitch axis in the required direction of the snap.
>
> [Section II, 8.9.3 b](#rb-snap_rolls.pitch_departure)

### Snap Exit Pitch Track {#snap_exit_track_y}

`snap_exit_track_y`

Checks that the snap does not leave the flight path pointing differently in pitch. Only an increase in the pitch error between the start and end of the snap is charged. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, high or wide in the box, or on awkward line angles.

??? note "Details"

    Immediately after autorotation the aircraft must be realigned with the prescribed line of flight, which may be on a parallel offset line. A misaligned flight path costs 0.5 point for each 5° of angular error in pitch, roll and yaw.

    FCScore compares the flight path direction with the template at the first and last points of the snap, in the pitch direction, and charges any increase in the absolute error between them. A snap that leaves the path closer to the template than it started is free, and an error present before the snap is not charged again. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 10° of error, in line with the IMAC rule of 0.5 point for each 5°.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side, and when the correct line is at an angle that is hard to picture: horizontal and vertical lines are the easiest to judge, 45° lines are harder and the angles in between are hardest. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> Immediately upon completion of autorotation, the aircraft must be realigned with the prescribed line of flight. … Any such misaligned flight path shall be downgraded at 0.5 for each 5 degrees of angular error from the prescribed line of flight in pitch, roll and yaw.
>
> [Section II, 8.9.3 g](#rb-snap_rolls.exit)

### Snap Exit Sideways Track {#snap_exit_track_z}

`snap_exit_track_z`

Checks that the snap does not leave the flight path pointing differently sideways. Only an increase in the sideways error between the start and end of the snap is charged. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, high or wide in the box, or on awkward line angles.

??? note "Details"

    Immediately after autorotation the aircraft must be realigned with the prescribed line of flight, which may be on a parallel offset line. A misaligned flight path costs 0.5 point for each 5° of angular error in pitch, roll and yaw.

    FCScore compares the flight path direction with the template at the first and last points of the snap, in the sideways direction, and charges any increase in the absolute error between them. A snap that leaves the path closer to the template than it started is free, and an error present before the snap is not charged again. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 10° of error, in line with the IMAC rule of 0.5 point for each 5°.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side, and when the correct line is at an angle that is hard to picture: horizontal and vertical lines are the easiest to judge, 45° lines are harder and the angles in between are hardest. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> Immediately upon completion of autorotation, the aircraft must be realigned with the prescribed line of flight. … Any such misaligned flight path shall be downgraded at 0.5 for each 5 degrees of angular error from the prescribed line of flight in pitch, roll and yaw.
>
> [Section II, 8.9.3 g](#rb-snap_rolls.exit)

### Stall Turn Pivot Width {#width}

`width`

Checks that the aircraft pivots near its centre of gravity at the top of a stall turn. The sideways travel in the direction of the turn beyond an allowance is charged, ignoring downwind drift. Small errors are discounted when hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, or when the aircraft is high or wide in the box.

??? note "Details"

    The aircraft must pivot around an axis no further from its centre of gravity than its wingtip, half a wingspan, and each additional half wingspan costs one point. No deduction is made for wind drift during the pivot, when the aircraft is stalled or nearly stalled.

    FCScore measures how far the aircraft's centre of gravity moves sideways in the direction of the turn from the start of the stall turn, with movement from drifting downwind removed but upwind drift left in. The largest width beyond a fixed allowance is charged once. FCScore uses a fixed distance rather than your wingspan, so it approximates the wingspan-based rule, and it charges smoothly rather than in half-wingspan steps.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight than across it, and when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side. Large errors are counted in full.

> To avoid a deduction, the aircraft must pivot around an axis point, which cannot be farther away from its center of gravity on the vertical up line than its wingtip (½ wingspans). The downgrade for this deviation is one (1) point per half wingspan that the point of rotation exceeds the maximum allowed (Fig 22).
>
> [Section II, 8.5](#rb-stall_turns.pivot)

> When the aircraft pivots at the top of the vertical line in a stalled or near stalled condition, no deduction shall be applied for wind drift during that particular time.
>
> [Section II, 8.5 f](#rb-stall_turns.wind_drift)

### Stall Turn Height Loss {#height}

`height`

Checks that the aircraft does not lose height through the pivot of a stall turn. How far below its highest point the aircraft is at the start and end of the stall turn, beyond an allowance, is charged. Small errors are discounted when hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, or when the aircraft is high or wide in the box.

??? note "Details"

    The aircraft should stop, then pivot, without a distinctive backward slide before the pivot starts, which zeroes the figure. A pivot away from the centre of gravity costs one point per half wingspan.

    FCScore measures how far below the highest point of the stall turn the aircraft is at the first and last points of the stall turn element, and charges any height lost beyond a fixed allowance. A slide back before the pivot or a drop through it shows up here. FCScore uses a fixed distance and charges a graded downgrade rather than the hard zero given in the rules for a distinct backward slide.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight than across it, and when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side. Large errors are counted in full.

> The maneuver shall also be zeroed if any distinctive backward sliding movement is observed before the start of the pivot, even if the rotation is correctly performed after the slide (Fig. 24).
>
> [Section II, 8.5](#rb-stall_turns.backslide)

> To avoid a deduction, the aircraft must pivot around an axis point, which cannot be farther away from its center of gravity on the vertical up line than its wingtip (½ wingspans). The downgrade for this deviation is one (1) point per half wingspan that the point of rotation exceeds the maximum allowed (Fig 22).
>
> [Section II, 8.5](#rb-stall_turns.pivot)

### Stall Turn Downline Pitch {#stallturn_exit_pitch}

`stallturn_exit_pitch`

Checks that the downline after a stall turn is truly vertical in pitch. The full pitch attitude error at the end of the line is charged once. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, high or wide in the box, or on awkward line angles.

??? note "Details"

    At the beginning and ending of the pivot the aircraft's attitude must be absolutely vertical, with no deviation in pitch or roll, and the lines are wind corrected so they are flown straight at the correct angle to the horizon.

    FCScore takes the last point of the line that follows the stall turn and charges the whole pitch angle between the fuselage and the template. It is an absolute measure at the end of the line. The IMAC guide judges the lines on flight path, whereas this downgrade looks at the nose attitude. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 10° of error, in line with the IMAC rule of 0.5 point for each 5°.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side, and when the correct line is at an angle that is hard to picture: horizontal and vertical lines are the easiest to judge, 45° lines are harder and the angles in between are hardest. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> During the pivot, the wings must remain in the vertical geometric plane as dictated by the ARESTI. This alignment must be maintained throughout the pivot, and the aircraft’s attitude at the beginning and the ending of the pivot must be absolutely vertical. During the pivot there must be no deviation in pitch or roll. Any pitch and roll deviation observed during the pivot shall be downgraded at 0.5 points for each 5 degrees of deviation.
>
> [Section II, 8.5](#rb-stall_turns.pivot_attitude)

> The up and down lines, vertical or 45 degree, must be wind corrected so that they are flown as a straight line at the correct angle to the horizon.
>
> [Section II, 8.5 a](#rb-stall_turns.wind_corrected)

### Tailslide Sideways Lean {#tailslide_yaw}

`tailslide_yaw`

Checks that the aircraft does not lean sideways during a tailslide. Only growth in the sideways lean of the fuselage is charged. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, or high or wide in the box.

??? note "Details"

    All lines and arcs of a tailslide must be wind corrected and correctly aligned within the airspace, and alignment deviations cost 0.5 point for each 5°.

    FCScore measures the lean of the fuselage sideways relative to the template throughout the tailslide and charges each increase in the absolute angle; a decrease is free. This is based on the direction the nose points (the attitude). FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 10° of error, in line with the IMAC rule of 0.5 point for each 5°.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, and when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> All lines and arcs flown in the maneuver are to be wind corrected and correctly aligned within the airspace as described in sections 5.3, 7.1 and 7.2. Observed alignment deviations receive a deduction of 0.5 points for each 5 degrees of deviation.
>
> [Section II, 8.6 a](#rb-tailslides.alignment)

### Tailslide Exit Pitch {#tailslide_exit_pitch}

`tailslide_exit_pitch`

Checks that the aircraft finishes the tailslide pointing vertically down in pitch. The full pitch attitude error at the end of the tailslide is charged once. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, high or wide in the box, or on awkward line angles.

??? note "Details"

    After sliding backwards the aircraft must fall through in the appropriate direction without the nose moving off axis, recover on the plane of entry, and establish a visible vertical down line.

    FCScore takes the last point of the tailslide and charges the whole pitch angle between the fuselage and the template. It is an absolute measure at that point, so a swing past the vertical that has settled by then is not charged. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 10° of error, in line with the IMAC rule of 0.5 point for each 5°.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side, and when the correct line is at an angle that is hard to picture: horizontal and vertical lines are the easiest to judge, 45° lines are harder and the angles in between are hardest. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> After performing the Tail Slide at the peak of the maneuver, the aircraft must establish a visible vertical down line. If this line is omitted, a downgrade of one (1) point is to be applied.
>
> [Section II, 8.6 g](#rb-tailslides.downline)

> All lines and arcs flown in the maneuver are to be wind corrected and correctly aligned within the airspace as described in sections 5.3, 7.1 and 7.2. Observed alignment deviations receive a deduction of 0.5 points for each 5 degrees of deviation.
>
> [Section II, 8.6 a](#rb-tailslides.alignment)

### Tailslide Stop {#tailslide_stop}

`tailslide_stop`

Checks that the aircraft comes to a stop at the top of the vertical line before it slides back. The vertical speed left at the end of the upline is charged once. Small errors are discounted when hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, or when the aircraft is high or wide in the box.

??? note "Details"

    The aircraft must make a smooth and steady transition up to vertical flight and come to a complete stop in that attitude before sliding backwards.

    FCScore takes the last point of the line before the tailslide and charges the absolute vertical speed there. A larger speed means the aircraft was still climbing, or already falling, instead of being stopped. The downgrade scale is an FCScore value; the rules do not set a speed limit.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight than across it, and when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side. Large errors are counted in full.

> In summary, the aircraft shall make a smooth and steady transition up to vertical flight, and the aircraft shall come to a complete stop in this attitude.
>
> [Section II, 8.6](#rb-tailslides.stop)

### Tailslide Slide Distance {#tailslide_drop}

`tailslide_drop`

Checks that the aircraft slides backwards a visible distance. A slide shorter than 1 m is charged. Small errors are discounted when hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, or when the aircraft is high or wide in the box.

??? note "Details"

    At the point when the aircraft stops climbing it must slide backwards a visible amount in the vertical plane; if there is no visible backward slide the whole figure is zeroed.

    FCScore adds up the distance travelled backwards through the tailslide and charges any shortfall below 1 m. FCScore uses a fixed distance for 'visible' and charges a graded downgrade rather than the zero given in the rules.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight than across it, and when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side. Large errors are counted in full.

> At the point when the aircraft stops climbing, it must slide backwards a visible amount in the vertical plane.
>
> [Section II, 8.6](#rb-tailslides.slide)

> Absence of any visible backward slide in the vertical plane zero’s the entire maneuver.
>
> [Section II, 8.6 b](#rb-tailslides.zero)

### Sequence Entry Yaw {#seqstart_entry_track_z}

`seqstart_entry_track_z`

Checks the heading before the first figure. The error at the start of the window, just before the figure, is charged in full. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, high or wide in the box, or on awkward line angles.

??? note "Details"

    The first figure of a sequence begins as the aircraft leaves wings-level horizontal flight, and every figure begins on a definite horizontal line. Nothing is judged before the first figure, so FCScore looks at the last second of the line before it, to make sure the aircraft enters the figure on a level, aligned path and does not dive, climb or bank into it.

    FCScore takes the sample one second before the start of the first element of the figure and charges the whole heading (yaw) angle between the direction of travel and the template. It is an absolute measure because nothing earlier has been charged. The window length is a tuning setting (one second by default). FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 10° of error, in line with the IMAC rule of 0.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side, and when the correct line is at an angle that is hard to picture: horizontal and vertical lines are the easiest to judge, 45° lines are harder and the angles in between are hardest. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> All figures begin and end on definite horizontal lines, and both must be present in order to earn a good grade.
>
> [Section II, 7.1](#rb-lines.entry_exit)

> The first figure of a sequence begins at the moment the aircraft departs from its wings-level, horizontal flight path.
>
> [Section II, 6.2](#rb-lines.figure_start)

### Sequence Entry Yaw Drift {#seqstart_track_z}

`seqstart_track_z`

Checks the heading stays correct before the first figure. Only growth in the error over the window next to the figure is charged, so a correction back towards the template is free. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, high or wide in the box, or on awkward line angles.

??? note "Details"

    The first figure of a sequence begins as the aircraft leaves wings-level horizontal flight, and every figure begins on a definite horizontal line. Nothing is judged before the first figure, so FCScore looks at the last second of the line before it, to make sure the aircraft enters the figure on a level, aligned path and does not dive, climb or bank into it.

    FCScore measures the heading (yaw) angle between the direction of travel and the template over the last second of the line before the figure and charges each increase in the absolute error; a decrease is free. An error already present at the start of the window is charged by the matching check at that point, not again here. The window ends where the figure starts and moves with it, so the error cannot be moved out of the score by placing the start of the figure later. The window length is a tuning setting (one second by default). FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 10° of error, in line with the IMAC rule of 0.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side, and when the correct line is at an angle that is hard to picture: horizontal and vertical lines are the easiest to judge, 45° lines are harder and the angles in between are hardest. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> All figures begin and end on definite horizontal lines, and both must be present in order to earn a good grade.
>
> [Section II, 7.1](#rb-lines.entry_exit)

> The first figure of a sequence begins at the moment the aircraft departs from its wings-level, horizontal flight path.
>
> [Section II, 6.2](#rb-lines.figure_start)
