### Sequence Entry Wings Level {#seqstart_entry_roll_angle}

`seqstart_entry_roll_angle`

Checks the roll angle before the first figure. The error at the start of the window, just before the figure, is charged in full. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: when you are looking at the top or underside of the aircraft, when it is high or wide in the box, or at awkward bank angles.

??? note "Details"

    The first figure of a sequence begins as the aircraft leaves wings-level horizontal flight, and every figure begins on a definite horizontal line. Nothing is judged before the first figure, so FCScore looks at the last second of the line before it, to make sure the aircraft enters the figure on a level, aligned path and does not dive, climb or bank into it.

    FCScore takes the sample one second before the start of the first element of the figure and charges the whole difference between the aircraft's roll angle and the template attitude. It is an absolute measure because nothing earlier has been charged. The window length is a tuning setting (one second by default). FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 10° of error, in line with the IMAC rule of 0.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. Roll errors are easiest to see when the aircraft is viewed side-on and hardest when you are looking at its top or underside. They are also harder to judge when the aircraft is high in the box or far to one side, and when the bank angle or the line is awkward to picture: wings level, knife-edge and inverted are the easiest references, with the angles in between the hardest. A fixed balancing factor, smaller than for flight path errors, further reduces small roll errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> All figures begin and end on definite horizontal lines, and both must be present in order to earn a good grade.
>
> [Section II, 7.1](#rb-lines.entry_exit)

> The first figure of a sequence begins at the moment the aircraft departs from its wings-level, horizontal flight path.
>
> [Section II, 6.2](#rb-lines.figure_start)

> On the other hand, any bank angle of the wing in the roll axis should be downgraded using the standard rule of 0.5 point deduction per 5 degrees
>
> [Section II, 5.3](#rb-general.bank)

### Sequence Exit Yaw {#seqend_exit_track_z}

`seqend_exit_track_z`

Checks the heading after the last figure. The error at the end of the figure is charged in full. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, high or wide in the box, or on awkward line angles.

??? note "Details"

    The last figure of a sequence ends when the aircraft returns to wings-level horizontal flight, and every figure ends on a definite horizontal line. Nothing is judged after the last figure, so FCScore looks at the first second of the line after it, to make sure the aircraft leaves the figure level and aligned and does not overshoot, dive, climb or bank away from it.

    FCScore takes the last point of the figure, the start of the exit line, and charges the whole heading (yaw) angle between the direction of travel and the template. It is an absolute measure because nothing earlier has been charged. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 10° of error, in line with the IMAC rule of 0.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side, and when the correct line is at an angle that is hard to picture: horizontal and vertical lines are the easiest to judge, 45° lines are harder and the angles in between are hardest. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> All figures begin and end on definite horizontal lines, and both must be present in order to earn a good grade.
>
> [Section II, 7.1](#rb-lines.entry_exit)

> If an aircraft does not return to wings-level, horizontal flight at the end of one fuselage length when exiting a figure, any deviation from wings level horizontal flight to the track on the line of the following figure MUST be deducted from the score of the figure in progress using the ½ point per 5 degrees rule.
>
> [Section II, 6.2](#rb-lines.figure_exit)

> On the other hand, any bank angle of the wing in the roll axis should be downgraded using the standard rule of 0.5 point deduction per 5 degrees
>
> [Section II, 5.3](#rb-general.bank)

### Sequence Exit Roll Angle {#seqend_roll_angle}

`seqend_roll_angle`

Checks the roll angle stays correct after the last figure. Only growth in the error over the window next to the figure is charged, so a correction back towards the template is free. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: when you are looking at the top or underside of the aircraft, when it is high or wide in the box, or at awkward bank angles.

??? note "Details"

    The last figure of a sequence ends when the aircraft returns to wings-level horizontal flight, and every figure ends on a definite horizontal line. Nothing is judged after the last figure, so FCScore looks at the first second of the line after it, to make sure the aircraft leaves the figure level and aligned and does not overshoot, dive, climb or bank away from it.

    FCScore measures the difference between the aircraft's roll angle and the template attitude over the first second of the line after the figure and charges each increase in the absolute error; a decrease is free. An error already present at the start of the window is charged by the matching check at the end of the figure, not again here. The window starts where the figure ends and moves with it, so an overshoot cannot be moved out of the score by ending the figure earlier. The window length is a tuning setting (one second by default). FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 10° of error, in line with the IMAC rule of 0.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. Roll errors are easiest to see when the aircraft is viewed side-on and hardest when you are looking at its top or underside. They are also harder to judge when the aircraft is high in the box or far to one side, and when the bank angle or the line is awkward to picture: wings level, knife-edge and inverted are the easiest references, with the angles in between the hardest. A fixed balancing factor, smaller than for flight path errors, further reduces small roll errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> All figures begin and end on definite horizontal lines, and both must be present in order to earn a good grade.
>
> [Section II, 7.1](#rb-lines.entry_exit)

> If an aircraft does not return to wings-level, horizontal flight at the end of one fuselage length when exiting a figure, any deviation from wings level horizontal flight to the track on the line of the following figure MUST be deducted from the score of the figure in progress using the ½ point per 5 degrees rule.
>
> [Section II, 6.2](#rb-lines.figure_exit)

> On the other hand, any bank angle of the wing in the roll axis should be downgraded using the standard rule of 0.5 point deduction per 5 degrees
>
> [Section II, 5.3](#rb-general.bank)

## Positioning (box) downgrades

### Box Ceiling {#top}

`top`

Checks that the figure stays inside the top of the box. The distance outside, averaged over the duration of the figure, is charged, so a small or brief excursion costs little. Small excursions that are hard to see are discounted.

??? note "Details"

    Judges give an overall Airspace Control score for placing the figures so that they can be optimally judged at all times, with a tight footprint. Flying so far away that the aircraft is difficult to judge scores poorly.

    FCScore measures how far the aircraft is outside the top of the box over the whole figure. Each stretch outside is charged in proportion to how far out it is and for how much of the figure's duration; the floor is charged on a steeper scale. The IMAC guide does not define the dimensions of the box or give a per-figure downgrade for leaving it, so the box used here and the amount charged are FCScore's own estimate of airspace control.

    Visibility is based on the direction of the error compared with the direction of view: an error that lies along the line of sight is hard to see, one across it is easier, so small excursions are discounted when they are hard to see. Large excursions are counted in full.

> The highest standard for Airspace Control will be the pilot that exhibits a significant ability to control the location of the aircraft inside the airspace, relative to the judges, which results in a tight footprint and has the aircraft such that it can be optimally judged at all times.
>
> [Section II, 4.3](#rb-airspace.control)

### Front Box Boundary {#front}

`front`

Checks that the figure stays behind the front boundary of the box, which is placed at the deadline. The distance in front of the boundary, averaged over the duration of the figure, is charged, so a small or brief excursion costs little. Small excursions that are hard to see are discounted.

??? note "Details"

    The deadline is 100 feet (30.5 m) in front of the contestant, and any maneuver where the aircraft completely or partially crosses it is zeroed for safety reasons.

    FCScore measures how far the aircraft is in front of the front boundary of the box over the whole figure. Each stretch in front is charged in proportion to how far in front it is and for how much of the figure's duration. The rules zero a figure that crosses the deadline, whereas FCScore charges a graded downgrade, so it is only an estimate of the severity. The IMAC guide does not define the dimensions of the box or give a per-figure downgrade for leaving it, so the box used here and the amount charged are FCScore's own estimate of airspace control.

    Visibility is based on the direction of the error compared with the direction of view: an error that lies along the line of sight is hard to see, one across it is easier, so small excursions are discounted when they are hard to see. Large excursions are counted in full.

> The “Deadline” is located 100 feet (30.5 meters) in front of the contestant.
>
> [Section II, 4.2](#rb-airspace.deadline_location)

> The judges shall zero (0) any maneuver where the aircraft completely or partially crosses the deadline.
>
> [Section II, 4.2](#rb-airspace.deadline)

## Inter-element downgrades

### Loop Radius Matching {#inter.loop_radius}

`inter.loop_radius`

Checks that the loops and part-loops in a figure that must have the same radius do match. Each radius is compared with the one before it and the percentage difference is charged. Differences are discounted for small elements, which are harder to compare: visibility rises with the distance flown relative to the height of the box.

??? note "Details"

    Where the radii of part-loops are required to be the same and they are not, one point is deducted for each mismatch, with the first part-loop flown as the standard. The size of a loop is not a criterion, only whether the radii match where the figure requires it.

    FCScore takes the radius of each loop the figure requires to match and compares each with the previous one, rather than with the first, charging in proportion to how many times larger one is than the other. A pair that matches scores zero, whatever the size. Whether each loop is round is judged by Loop Roundness.

    Visibility scales the whole downgrade, not only small differences. Each comparison is weighted by how large the elements are compared with the height of the aerobatic box, taking the more visible of the two elements being compared: an element that fills the box is fully visible, while a small one is proportionally harder to judge against its neighbour.

> Where radii of part loops within these figures are required to be the same and they are not, a downgrade of one (1) point is to be applied for each mismatch. The standard is the first part loop flown within the figure.
>
> [Section II, 8.7.1 c](#rb-loops.matching_radii)

### Line Length Matching {#inter.line_length}

`inter.line_length`

Checks that lines that must be of equal length in a figure are. Each length is compared with the one before it and the percentage difference is charged. Differences are discounted for small elements, which are harder to compare: visibility rises with the distance flown relative to the height of the box.

??? note "Details"

    Interior lines do not have to be equal unless the figure says so, as in Family 3 and the square and octagon loops. Where equal lengths are required, a visible variation costs one point, a 1:2 difference two points, and so on up to three, with the first line flown as the basis.

    FCScore takes the length of each line the figure requires to match and compares each with the previous one, charging in proportion to how many times longer one is than the other. A pair that matches scores zero, whatever the length. FCScore's scale is smooth rather than in the rulebook's steps.

    Visibility scales the whole downgrade, not only small differences. Each comparison is weighted by how large the elements are compared with the height of the aerobatic box, taking the more visible of the two elements being compared: an element that fills the box is fully visible, while a small one is proportionally harder to judge against its neighbour.

> If within a figure two or more lines must be of the same length, an observed variation is penalized by the grade in the following manner (Fig. 14): … A visible variation = 1 point deduction … If the lengths vary by 1:2 = 2 point deduction … And so forth up to a 3 point deduction
>
> [Section II, 7.1](#rb-lines.length_penalty)

> The basis for judging line length is the first line flown.
>
> [Section II, 7.1](#rb-lines.length_basis)

### Roll Pause Matching {#inter.point_length}

`inter.point_length`

Checks that the pauses between the rolls or points of a roll combination are of the same length. Each length is compared with the one before it and the percentage difference is charged. Differences are discounted for small elements, which are harder to compare: visibility rises with the distance flown relative to the height of the box.

??? note "Details"

    In point rolls the pauses must be identical, and each visible variation in the pause segments costs one point. Unlinked rolling elements must show a brief but perceptible pause between them.

    FCScore takes the distance flown in each pause of a roll combination on the same line and compares each with the previous one, charging in proportion to how many times longer one is than the other. A pair that matches scores zero, whatever the length. The rules judge the duration of the pauses, while FCScore compares the distance flown during them.

    Visibility scales the whole downgrade, not only small differences. Each comparison is weighted by how large the elements are compared with the height of the aerobatic box, taking the more visible of the two elements being compared: an element that fills the box is fully visible, while a small one is proportionally harder to judge against its neighbour.

> Each visible variation in the duration of the pause segments is downgraded by one (1) point.
>
> [Section II, 8.9.2](#rb-rolls.point_pause)

> Unlinked rolling elements must show a brief but perceptible pause between the elements that comprise the rolling combination. Absence of a perceptible pause between elements of the combination shall be downgraded by 1 point.
>
> [Section II, 8.9](#rb-rolls.unlinked_pause)

### Roll Rate Matching {#inter.roll_rate}

`inter.roll_rate`

Checks that the rolls within one roll combination are flown at the same roll rate. Each rate is compared with the one before it and the percentage difference is charged. Differences are discounted for small elements, which are harder to compare: visibility rises with the distance flown relative to the height of the box.

??? note "Details"

    In point rolls the roll rate of each segment must match the preceding segment, and any visible deviation from one segment to the next costs one point per occurrence.

    FCScore takes the roll rate of each roll within a roll combination on the same line and compares each with the previous one, charging in proportion to how many times faster one is than the other. A pair that matches scores zero, whatever the rate. FCScore groups rolls by the figure definition rather than by the rule, so check the rulebook for your figure. Whether the rate is steady within one roll is judged by Roll Rate Consistency.

    Visibility scales the whole downgrade, not only small differences. Each comparison is weighted by how large the elements are compared with the height of the aerobatic box, taking the more visible of the two elements being compared: an element that fills the box is fully visible, while a small one is proportionally harder to judge against its neighbour.

> Any visible deviation in roll rate from one segment to the next, or within a segment, is to be downgraded by one (1) point per occurrence.
>
> [Section II, 8.9.2](#rb-rolls.point_rate)

### Roll Position On Line {#inter.pad_length}

`inter.pad_length`

Checks that a roll is centred on its line, with equal lengths of line before and after it. The two lengths are compared and the percentage difference is charged. Differences are discounted for small elements, which are harder to compare: visibility rises with the distance flown relative to the height of the box.

??? note "Details"

    Whenever any kind of roll is placed on an interior line, the lengths of the two parts of the line before and after the roll must be equal, with a visible variation costing one point and more for larger differences.

    FCScore compares the length of line before the roll with the length after, charging in proportion to how many times longer one is than the other. A roll that is perfectly centred scores zero, whatever the length of the line.

    Visibility scales the whole downgrade, not only small differences. Each comparison is weighted by how large the elements are compared with the height of the aerobatic box, taking the more visible of the two elements being compared: an element that fills the box is fully visible, while a small one is proportionally harder to judge against its neighbour.

> Whenever any kind of roll is placed on an interior line, the lengths of the two parts of the line before and after the roll must be equal.
>
> [Section II, 7.1](#rb-lines.length_equal)

> If within a figure two or more lines must be of the same length, an observed variation is penalized by the grade in the following manner (Fig. 14): … A visible variation = 1 point deduction … If the lengths vary by 1:2 = 2 point deduction … And so forth up to a 3 point deduction
>
> [Section II, 7.1](#rb-lines.length_penalty)

## Rulebook references

### Section II, 4.2 {#rb-airspace.deadline}

`airspace.deadline`

> The judges shall zero (0) any maneuver where the aircraft completely or partially crosses the deadline.

### Section II, 4.2 {#rb-airspace.deadline_location}

`airspace.deadline_location`

> The “Deadline” is located 100 feet (30.5 meters) in front of the contestant.

### Section II, 4.3 {#rb-airspace.control}

`airspace.control`

> The highest standard for Airspace Control will be the pilot that exhibits a significant ability to control the location of the aircraft inside the airspace, relative to the judges, which results in a tight footprint and has the aircraft such that it can be optimally judged at all times.

### Section II, 4.3 {#rb-airspace.poor_control}

`airspace.poor_control`

> The lowest standard for Airspace Control will be the pilot that exhibits a poor ability to control the location of the aircraft inside the airspace, relative to the judges, which results in an excessively large footprint and has the aircraft consistently so far away as to be difficult to properly judge.

### Section II, 5 {#rb-general.flight_path}

`general.flight_path`

> Judges should evaluate any maneuver focusing primarily on the aircraft flight path, but at the same time, also downgrade for any variation of the aircraft attitude that is not directly related to maintaining a correct flight path.

### Section II, 5.1 {#rb-general.flight_path_definition}

`general.flight_path_definition`

> Think of the aircraft condensed into a single dot and watch the path this dot takes through the sky. This is the flight path, or track, or the aircraft’s center of gravity. Judging the flight path consists of comparing the observed path with fixed references such as the horizon, or the X and Y-axis of the aerobatic airspace.

### Section II, 5.3 {#rb-general.bank}

`general.bank`

> On the other hand, any bank angle of the wing in the roll axis should be downgraded using the standard rule of 0.5 point deduction per 5 degrees

### Section II, 5.3 {#rb-general.drift}

`general.drift`

> Wind correction shall be used throughout the aerobatic airspace. Any drift observed on any line (horizontal, 45 degrees or vertical) shall be downgraded using the 0.5 point deduction per 5 degrees rule

### Section II, 5.3 {#rb-general.stalled}

`general.stalled`

> The only maneuvers that are not to be wind corrected are the ones involving a stalled condition, such as a Stall Turn (otherwise known as “Hammerhead”), Tail Slide, spin and snap roll(s) (otherwise known as a “flick roll”). During the period of time that the aircraft is in a stalled, or near stalled condition, any wind drift shall be disregarded by the judges and not downgraded.

### Section II, 5.3 {#rb-general.wind_correction}

`general.wind_correction`

> The general rule is that judges shall ignore any aircraft change of attitude required to maintain a correct flight path. At the same time, the usual 0.5 point deduction per 5 degrees of deviation shall be applied to anything that is not related with wind correcting.

### Section II, 6 {#rb-general.grading}

`general.grading`

> A grade of ten (10) represents a perfect figure in which the judge saw no deviations from prescribed criteria.

### Section II, 6.1 i {#rb-general.angle_rule}

`general.angle_rule`

> Speed of aircraft is not a criterion. A reduction of grade will be applied for each deviation from the prescribed criteria for the figure. The grade will be reduced by 0.5 points for each 5 degrees of deviation.

### Section II, 6.2 {#rb-lines.figure_exit}

`lines.figure_exit`

> If an aircraft does not return to wings-level, horizontal flight at the end of one fuselage length when exiting a figure, any deviation from wings level horizontal flight to the track on the line of the following figure MUST be deducted from the score of the figure in progress using the ½ point per 5 degrees rule.

### Section II, 6.2 {#rb-lines.figure_start}

`lines.figure_start`

> The first figure of a sequence begins at the moment the aircraft departs from its wings-level, horizontal flight path.

### Section II, 7.1 {#rb-lines.entry_exit}

`lines.entry_exit`

> All figures begin and end on definite horizontal lines, and both must be present in order to earn a good grade.

### Section II, 7.1 {#rb-lines.flight_path}

`lines.flight_path`

> All lines are judged in relation to the true horizon and the axes of the Aerobatic Airspace. Horizontal and Vertical lines are judged primarily on flight path (Ref Rule 5.3 for wind correction criteria).

### Section II, 7.1 {#rb-lines.length_basis}

`lines.length_basis`

> The basis for judging line length is the first line flown.

### Section II, 7.1 {#rb-lines.length_equal}

`lines.length_equal`

> Whenever any kind of roll is placed on an interior line, the lengths of the two parts of the line before and after the roll must be equal.

### Section II, 7.1 {#rb-lines.length_penalty}

`lines.length_penalty`

> If within a figure two or more lines must be of the same length, an observed variation is penalized by the grade in the following manner (Fig. 14): … A visible variation = 1 point deduction … If the lengths vary by 1:2 = 2 point deduction … And so forth up to a 3 point deduction

### Section II, 8.2.1 a {#rb-turns.entry_bank}

`turns.entry_bank`

> The angle of bank established by the initial rolling maneuver must be at least 60 degrees and not greater than 90 degrees. Any less or more is a 0.5 point deduction for every 5 degrees.

### Section II, 8.2.1 b {#rb-turns.bank}

`turns.bank`

> The angle of bank, once established, must remain constant. Any deviation is a 0.5 point deduction for every 5 degrees of deviation.

### Section II, 8.2.1 d {#rb-turns.altitude}

`turns.altitude`

> The aircraft must maintain a constant altitude throughout the figure. Any variation would be 0.5 point deduction for every 5 degrees of change.

### Section II, 8.2.2 c {#rb-turns.rolling_stoppage}

`turns.rolling_stoppage`

> Each stoppage of the rate of roll is a deduction of one (1) point.

### Section II, 8.2.2 d {#rb-turns.rolling_rate}

`turns.rolling_rate`

> Each variation in the rate of roll is a one (1) point deduction.

### Section II, 8.5 {#rb-stall_turns.backslide}

`stall_turns.backslide`

> The maneuver shall also be zeroed if any distinctive backward sliding movement is observed before the start of the pivot, even if the rotation is correctly performed after the slide (Fig. 24).

### Section II, 8.5 {#rb-stall_turns.pivot}

`stall_turns.pivot`

> To avoid a deduction, the aircraft must pivot around an axis point, which cannot be farther away from its center of gravity on the vertical up line than its wingtip (½ wingspans). The downgrade for this deviation is one (1) point per half wingspan that the point of rotation exceeds the maximum allowed (Fig 22).

### Section II, 8.5 {#rb-stall_turns.pivot_attitude}

`stall_turns.pivot_attitude`

> During the pivot, the wings must remain in the vertical geometric plane as dictated by the ARESTI. This alignment must be maintained throughout the pivot, and the aircraft’s attitude at the beginning and the ending of the pivot must be absolutely vertical. During the pivot there must be no deviation in pitch or roll. Any pitch and roll deviation observed during the pivot shall be downgraded at 0.5 points for each 5 degrees of deviation.

### Section II, 8.5 a {#rb-stall_turns.wind_corrected}

`stall_turns.wind_corrected`

> The up and down lines, vertical or 45 degree, must be wind corrected so that they are flown as a straight line at the correct angle to the horizon.

### Section II, 8.5 b {#rb-stall_turns.lines}

`stall_turns.lines`

> On the up and down lines, any roll deviation, or deviation of the track of the aircraft in pitch or yaw will result in a deduction of 0.5 points per 5 degrees of deviation.

### Section II, 8.5 f {#rb-stall_turns.wind_drift}

`stall_turns.wind_drift`

> When the aircraft pivots at the top of the vertical line in a stalled or near stalled condition, no deduction shall be applied for wind drift during that particular time.

### Section II, 8.6 {#rb-tailslides.slide}

`tailslides.slide`

> At the point when the aircraft stops climbing, it must slide backwards a visible amount in the vertical plane.

### Section II, 8.6 {#rb-tailslides.stop}

`tailslides.stop`

> In summary, the aircraft shall make a smooth and steady transition up to vertical flight, and the aircraft shall come to a complete stop in this attitude.

### Section II, 8.6 a {#rb-tailslides.alignment}

`tailslides.alignment`

> All lines and arcs flown in the maneuver are to be wind corrected and correctly aligned within the airspace as described in sections 5.3, 7.1 and 7.2. Observed alignment deviations receive a deduction of 0.5 points for each 5 degrees of deviation.

### Section II, 8.6 b {#rb-tailslides.zero}

`tailslides.zero`

> Absence of any visible backward slide in the vertical plane zero’s the entire maneuver.

### Section II, 8.6 c {#rb-tailslides.roll}

`tailslides.roll`

> On all up and down lines, the roll attitude must be perpendicular to the plane of the main axis of flight, either the X or Y axis. This includes the duration of the fall through. Watch for the aircraft torqueing off the correct plane of flight. Any deviation in roll shall be downgraded at 0.5 points per five (5) degrees of deviation.

### Section II, 8.6 g {#rb-tailslides.downline}

`tailslides.downline`

> After performing the Tail Slide at the peak of the maneuver, the aircraft must establish a visible vertical down line. If this line is omitted, a downgrade of one (1) point is to be applied.

### Section II, 8.7.1 a {#rb-loops.size}

`loops.size`

> The size of a loop or part loop is not a grading criterion.

### Section II, 8.7.1 b {#rb-loops.constant_radius}

`loops.constant_radius`

> All radii are to be constant. Each visible variation in the radii in a loop or part loop is to be downgraded by one (1) point. Flight path without any radius (straight line or “flat spot”), is deducted at one point per occurrence.

### Section II, 8.7.1 c {#rb-loops.matching_radii}

`loops.matching_radii`

> Where radii of part loops within these figures are required to be the same and they are not, a downgrade of one (1) point is to be applied for each mismatch. The standard is the first part loop flown within the figure.

### Section II, 8.7.4a {#rb-loops.integrated_rolls}

`loops.integrated_rolls`

> If there is a rolling element (roll, point rolls or snap roll) at the apex of the loop, it must be centered in the loop and flown on the arc of the loop itself (Fig. 38). Flying the roll on a line at the apex of the loop is at least a two (2) point downgrade. If the roll is not centered, it must be downgraded 0.5 points for every five degrees that it is off center.

### Section II, 8.7.4a {#rb-loops.perpendicular}

`loops.perpendicular`

> Therefore, a standard deduction of 0.5 points per five (5) degrees shall be applied if the finish point is displaced in a direction perpendicular to the plane of the loop (Fig. 34). In a heavy crosswind situation, a loop might be flown with visible crabbing and no deduction shall be applied in this case.

### Section II, 8.7.4a {#rb-loops.roll}

`loops.roll`

> Aircraft displaying any roll other than during a roll element on the loop, 0.5 point per five degrees of roll.

### Section II, 8.9 {#rb-rolls.constant_rate}

`rolls.constant_rate`

> In all cases, the same criteria apply: the rate of roll must be constant throughout the roll(s). The aircraft shall continue to project, during the rolling portion, the prescribed plane and direction of flight.

### Section II, 8.9 {#rb-rolls.unlinked_pause}

`rolls.unlinked_pause`

> Unlinked rolling elements must show a brief but perceptible pause between the elements that comprise the rolling combination. Absence of a perceptible pause between elements of the combination shall be downgraded by 1 point.

### Section II, 8.9.1 {#rb-rolls.finish}

`rolls.finish`

> The finish of the roll must be as crisp and precise as possible. Coming to a slow finish in fact represents a change in the rate of roll and shall be penalized accordingly.

### Section II, 8.9.1 {#rb-rolls.rate}

`rolls.rate`

> The penalty for varying the rate of roll is one (1) point per variation. Any stoppage in the roll that could result its being considered a point roll would zero (0) the figure.

### Section II, 8.9.1 {#rb-rolls.stop}

`rolls.stop`

> The wing must stop precisely after the desired degree of rotation and not go past the stop point and then return. This is referred to as “bumping the point” and a deduction of 0.5 points per 5 degrees shall be given in this case.

### Section II, 8.9.2 {#rb-rolls.point_pause}

`rolls.point_pause`

> Each visible variation in the duration of the pause segments is downgraded by one (1) point.

### Section II, 8.9.2 {#rb-rolls.point_rate}

`rolls.point_rate`

> Any visible deviation in roll rate from one segment to the next, or within a segment, is to be downgraded by one (1) point per occurrence.

### Section II, 8.9.2 {#rb-rolls.point_rotation}

`rolls.point_rotation`

> Errors in degrees of rotation (under/over rotating the points) are downgraded at a half (.5) point per five (5) degrees.

### Section II, 8.9.3 {#rb-snap_rolls.autorotation_definition}

`snap_rolls.autorotation_definition`

> Autorotation: State of flight in which the aircraft is rolling while also displaced from straight flight (or radius in loops and part loops) in both the pitch and yaw axes.

### Section II, 8.9.3 b {#rb-snap_rolls.pitch_departure}

`snap_rolls.pitch_departure`

> There must be an observable departure in the pitch axis in the required direction of the snap.

### Section II, 8.9.3 c {#rb-snap_rolls.yaw_component}

`snap_rolls.yaw_component`

> Autorotation may difficult to discern, but there will be a visible yaw displacement to the rotation. Lacking any observable yaw component, the aircraft will be rotating only on its roll axis and not presenting a snap.

### Section II, 8.9.3 d {#rb-snap_rolls.pre_rotation}

`snap_rolls.pre_rotation`

> Any rotation / roll observed prior to the required pitch movement is to be downgraded 0 .5 points for each 5 degrees of such rotation.

### Section II, 8.9.3 f {#rb-snap_rolls.autorotation_maintained}

`snap_rolls.autorotation_maintained`

> Autorotation, once initiated, must be maintained to the prescribed finish point of the snap roll. Exiting autorotation early and completing the snap with ailerons is a common error. In these cases, a downgrade of 0.5 points for each 5 degrees of rotation remaining at the point the autorotation ends shall apply.

### Section II, 8.9.3 g {#rb-snap_rolls.exit}

`snap_rolls.exit`

> Immediately upon completion of autorotation, the aircraft must be realigned with the prescribed line of flight. … Any such misaligned flight path shall be downgraded at 0.5 for each 5 degrees of angular error from the prescribed line of flight in pitch, roll and yaw.

### Section II, 8.9.4 {#rb-spins.stall_break}

`spins.stall_break`

> When the aircraft stalls, the nose will fall and at the same time a wing tip will drop in the direction of the spin initiating autorotation. The fall of the nose and the drop of the wing are to occur simultaneously. Failure to achieve this is to be considered a “late entry” and is to be downgraded.

### Section II, 8.9.4 {#rb-spins.stop_heading}

`spins.stop_heading`

> After completion of the prescribed number of turns, the aircraft must stop rotating precisely on the prescribed heading and then a wind corrected vertical down line must be shown.

### Section II, 8.9.4 f {#rb-spins.autorotation}

`spins.autorotation`

> The rotation in a spin must be autorotation which can be difficult to discern. A clue to making the judgment on "autorotation or not" is that autorotation will have a visible yaw component to the rotation. Absent this yaw component, it is probable that the aircraft is in some kind of an aileron roll. If a judge is certain that no autorotation occurred, a zero (0) is to be given.

### Section II, 8.9.4 g {#rb-spins.completion}

`spins.completion`

> Note that autorotation must carry to completion. It is common to see a pilot come out of autorotation early and aileron to the finish of the spin. If this occurs a penalty of 0.5 points per 5 degrees is to be applied for the amount of “aileroning” used to complete the required rotation.

### Section II, 8.9.4 g {#rb-spins.stop}

`spins.stop`

> The spin element must complete precisely at the degree of rotation called for by the ARESTI and not be short or beyond the prescribed end point of the rotation. Any deviation is to be downgraded 0.5 points per 5 degrees that the aircraft completes the spin short or long of the prescribed stopping point.

### Section II, 8.9.4 h {#rb-spins.downline}

`spins.downline`

> Upon completion of the prescribed degree of rotation a vertical down line is to be shown. Omission of this line is to be downgraded one (1) point.
